newsitem.title: UK: London jazz club owner Ronnie Scott dies at 69.
newsitem.headline: London jazz club owner Ronnie Scott dies at 69.

text.p: Ronnie Scott, the jazz saxophonist whose London club became a mecca for the most famous jazz musicians in the world, collapsed and died at his London home at the age of 69.
Friends said on Tuesday that Scott, who founded the club bearing his name in Soho in 1959, was found dead on Monday. The cause of his death was not immediately known.
Tributes from the jazz world poured in for Scott, whose roll-call of stars at the club ranged from Dizzie Gillespie and Sarah Vaughan to Django Reinhardt and Jimi Hendrix.
"He was a great character as well as a wonderful musician."

"(the club) was known all over the world....If a jazz musician anywhere wanted to come to London, the place he asked for first of all was Ronnie Scott's," said friend and fellow musician Johnny Dankworth.

Scott, known for his wacky sense of humour and for dressing all in black, started playing at the age of 13 and was inspired to open his club after discovering the jazz scene in New York after World War Two.
The Soho venue was an all-night taxi drivers' cafe before Scott took it over.
"We brought in a few second-hand chairs, some paints and brushes and a second-hand piano and that was it," he said in a recent radio interview.

"I don't think I'm much of a businessman. I'm a musician. If there's any winning formula it's because we present the best jazz in the world, it's comfortable and not overly expensive. Because I'm a musician I know what musicians require," said Scott.
The club is credited as the birthplace of the British jazz scene but it was the appearance of major stars from the United States which made it take off.

It was the first time that players such as Dexter Gordon, Coleman Hawkins and Art Blakey had been seen in Britain in an intimate club atmosphere and regular customers in the 1960s included the Rolling Stones, the Beatles and Rod Stewart.
Scott had a flair for unorthodox pairings. He once put Barney Kessel together with leading British classical guitarist John Williams, and put on Jimi Hendrix the week before he died.
Scott and his business partner Pete King staved off two financial crises in the 1980s and until last week Scott was still hosting acts at the club although he had recently stopped performing himself.
Far from glamorous with its red vinyl-padded bar, whitewashed walls and gingham covered tables, the club had a special atmosphere spiced with Scott's silly jokes.
He often introduced perfomers with the catchphrase "Quiet please, you're not here to enjoy yourselves."
On other nights, he would tell audiences "You're a great crowd tonight. Stone dead but great."

Scott was born in east London in 1927 and learnt to play the saxophone in his teens. He started work at 14 in a music shop and joined the Johnny Claes band in 1944 before going on to play with Ted Heath, Bert Ambrose and other popular dance band leaders.
He formed his own band in 1953 and toured in the United States, Paris and Vienna before opening his club in 1959 in Soho's Gerrard Street. It moved to the present Frith Street venue in 1968.

The show went on at the club on Monday night despite Scott's death. "He was a very funny man as well as a fabulous musician. He was also very sincere, that is why people took to him so readily," said James Parsons, a manager at the club.
A self-effacing man who never married, Scott was awarded the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in 1981 for services to jazz.
He promptly dubbed it the award for Other Bastards Efforts.
